opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of the debate around whether language models "understand" or have "meaning" ends up going in circles because people are working with very different, often implicit, notions of what meaning is. If you define meaning in a way that's maximally demanding, something like "meaning requires conscious intentional states directed at the world," then the question becomes uninteresting in a sense. You've basically settled it by definition, and there's nothing empirical left to do.

So the way I like to think about it is to borrow from the more formal, model-theoretic tradition in semantics, and also from the more use-based traditions. One useful starting point is that the meaning of a sentence is something like its truth conditions, or more generally the relationship between an utterance and the states of the world it's compatible with. Under that view, you can ask a concrete question: does a model trained only on text build internal representations that track the states of the world that sentences describe? Does it represent, for instance, which entities are present in a situation, what their properties are, how they change as a discourse unfolds?

And that's a question you can actually go and test. You can probe a model's representations, intervene on them, and see whether manipulating some internal state changes the model's predictions in the way you'd expect if that state encoded something about the world being described. Some of the work my group and others have done suggests that, at least in limited domains, you do find representations like this. They're imperfect and partial, but they're there.

The other piece is that I don't think grounding has to be all or nothing. There's a tendency to say "this model never touched the world, so its words can't refer to anything." But humans learn a huge amount of what they know about the world through language too. Most of what I know about, say, the structure of a cell or the history of some country, I never perceived directly. The text a model sees is produced by people who were grounded, and a lot of the structure of the world leaks into the statistics of that text. So a more interesting question is: how much of meaning is recoverable from the distribution of text alone, which parts aren't, and what additional signal, perception, interaction, action, feedback, you need to fill in the gaps.

So my answer is: define meaning in a way that makes it a measurable relation between representations and the world, rather than a metaphysical property, and then grounding becomes a graded, empirical question about what models represent and how they came to represent it. That's a question I think we can make real progress on.

r001.rationale: The response says text statistics inherit structure from human-grounded language, but it does not state that current models satisfy a causal theory of meaning through that connection.

r002.rationale: It says a definition requiring conscious intentional states settles the issue by definition, but it does not discuss human qualitative perceptual experience as the requirement that excludes text-only models.

r003.rationale: The response proposes measuring relations between representations and the world, but does not claim that an isomorphic representation of the real world is sufficient for grounding.

r004.rationale: It asks what can be recovered from text and what extra signals fill gaps, but does not identify training conditions under which models acquire representations structurally equivalent to human representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where the conversation gets confused a lot, because people are using the word "meaning" to mean a bunch of different things, and depending on which one you pick, the grounding question either becomes trivial or becomes impossible.

So one version of the question is sort of the philosophy-of-language version, where meaning is this relation between a symbol and something out in the world, and the worry is that a model that's only ever seen text can't possibly have that relation because the text was never connected to the world on the model's side. And I think if you define it that way, the answer is kind of baked in. Of course the model doesn't have it, it never touched anything, end of discussion. That's not a very interesting scientific question, it's just a definitional one.

The version I find more productive is a more functional or, I guess, more internalist notion. If you look at how people think about meaning in cognitive science, or honestly in a lot of the formal semantics tradition, what you care about is something like: does the system have an internal representation that behaves the way a representation of the world would behave? So does it track what's true in some situation, does it update that state as it gets more sentences, does it support the kinds of inferences that you'd expect if the thing actually understood what the sentences were about, rather than just what they were correlated with.

And the nice thing about defining it that way is that it turns into something you can actually go measure. You can build a little world, a grid world or some set of entities and relations, describe it in language, feed that to the model, and then go look inside and ask whether there's some part of the model's representation that corresponds to the state of that world. Not just "can it predict the next token," but is there a map from the model's activations to the actual configuration of objects, and does that map stay consistent as the discourse evolves. If you can find that, that's a form of grounding, even though no pixels or robots were involved.

So my short answer is that I'd want to define meaning in terms of the structure of the model's internal state and the relationship between that state and the thing the language is about, rather than in terms of the causal history of how the model came to have that state. The causal history question is interesting for other reasons, but it's not what makes this a scientific question. The thing that makes it scientific is that you can be wrong about it, you can look and find that the representations aren't there, or that they're there for some kinds of worlds and not others, and that's exactly the kind of result I think we should be chasing.

r001.rationale: The response says causal history is not what makes grounding a scientific question; it does not claim models satisfy a causal theory through training documents.

r002.rationale: It says a world-linking definition rules text-only models out by definition, but does not identify human qualitative perceptual experience as the requirement.

r003.rationale: It proposes that an internal representation tracking the world's configuration, with a consistent map from activations to that configuration, counts as grounding.

r004.rationale: It proposes testing model representations in described worlds, but does not ask under what training conditions models acquire representations structurally equivalent to human ones.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to ask is: what do we want a definition of meaning to help us explain? If we start by defining meaning as a connection between words and something outside language, then we’ve already decided that a system trained only on text is missing something. That doesn’t yet tell us what it can do, or what that missing connection would buy us.

I’d rather break the question into more concrete pieces. Can a model track what a speaker is referring to? Can it distinguish what someone said from what they intended to communicate? Can it use an instruction to make a prediction or take an action in a new situation? Those are different abilities, and they might require different kinds of experience.

Then grounding becomes an interesting empirical question: which of those abilities can you acquire from text, and which improve—or become possible—when you can observe and interact with the world? Text itself contains a lot of information about the world because people produce it to communicate about their experiences. So we shouldn’t assume that learning from text means learning nothing about the things text describes.

What I’d like is a notion of meaning that gives us testable distinctions between systems, rather than a single boundary where we declare that one system has meaning and another doesn’t.

r001.rationale: The response says text contains information about the world because people communicate about their experiences, but it does not state that current models satisfy a causal theory of meaning through that social connection.

r002.rationale: It discusses defining meaning as a connection between words and the world, but does not address qualitative perceptual experience or explain that this definition excludes text-only models by stipulation without experimentation.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose that a representation isomorphic to the real world is sufficient for grounding.

r004.rationale: It asks which abilities text or world interaction enables, but does not ask under what training conditions models acquire representations structurally equivalent to human representations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start by asking what you want a definition of meaning to explain. One thing we do with language is communicate information about the world. Another is use it to get other people to do things. And another is reason privately about situations that we haven’t actually experienced. I’m not sure that a single notion of grounding captures everything that matters in all of those cases.

To make this a scientific question, I’d want to turn it into a question about particular relationships: between an expression and something in the world, or between an expression and a speaker’s intentions. Then we can ask what information a model has about those relationships, how it acquired that information, and whether it can use it in a new situation.

For example, if a model has only learned from text, what can it infer about the physical world from the descriptions people produce? What remains ambiguous, and what additional experience would resolve that ambiguity? Those seem like questions where we can design experiments and learn something. I find that more productive than deciding in advance that meaning requires a particular kind of experience and then asking whether a language model qualifies.

r001.rationale: The response discusses text-only learning and human-produced descriptions, but does not say current models satisfy a causal theory of meaning through training documents’ connection to social language use.

r002.rationale: It criticizes requiring a particular kind of experience in advance, but does not specifically identify qualitative perceptual experience as the requirement that excludes text-only models by stipulation.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose that a representation isomorphic to the real world is sufficient for grounding.

r004.rationale: It proposes empirical questions about what text-only models infer and how experience might resolve ambiguity, but does not ask when different training data produce representations structurally equivalent to human representations.
